title: Notes of Ministry - 81 - August 1979

paragraphs.text: Psalm 47: 4; Genesis 33: 12–14; 47: 7–10, It is in mind to speak about Jacob. That this verse in Psalm 47 speaks of ‘the excellency of Jacob whom He loved’, is very striking. You might have thought it would say ‘the excellency of Israel’, but it says “the excellency of Jacob”. Anyone that God loves is very interesting to us. Jacob is thus a very interesting and profitable person to think about, read about, and speak about. This verse is very impressive; it deals with our inheritance—“He hath chosen our inheritance for us, the excellency of Jacob whom he loved”. It is very fine that God has chosen our inheritance. We have not chosen it. Our localities would enter into that. God has chosen our inheritance in our localities. He has chosen our neighbours, perhaps not the ones we would have chosen, but He has chosen them. I suppose Jacob was not the kind of man one would have chosen for a neighbour. He was, in some ways, a bit slippery, and you might have to be careful making a deal with him as you might come off second best! But, nevertheless, whatever else you might say about Jacob, what the scripture says more than once is that God loved him. He was a twin brother of Esau, but God hated Esau and loved Jacob.

So it is right that we should have a look at Jacob and see some of the features in him that God found lovable. We would like to be like him in that respect. He was loved because of that about him that was lovable. We might not think Jacob was a very lovable man, but he was.
There was something excellent about Jacob that God loved. One would

covet that there might be some elements with us like those which God loved in Jacob and that were victorious. In spite of his deficiencies—and who of us has not got them?—this is a very triumphant psalm—“All ye peoples, clap your hands; shout unto God with the voice of triumph!” (Psalm 47: 1). What a fine note with which to have Jacob introduced into a psalm!

There is nothing apologetic about this, it is triumphant! It shows what the work of God is, that in spite of any admixture there may be along with it, in itself it is triumphant. Nothing can overcome the work of God; it is going through and has elements that are practical and recognisable and that we can imitate.

Now the first thing we are told about Jacob is that he was a supplanter. His name means that, and that is a lesson we have to learn too; but what we have to supplant is in ourselves. Jacob had to supplant his brother, and we do not want to do that. But we have to learn that there is that in us that has to be supplanted. There was what had to be reduced in Jacob through God’s discipline until he arrived at this excellency; what you end with in Jacob is par excellence, that is, he is the blesser of the greatest man on earth, and it says, “the inferior is blessed by the better”, Hebrews 7: 7. And then he ends as a worshipper, which is the great end for all of us.

Then there is encouragement for the young brethren. I think one of the earliest features that God was pleased with in Jacob, so that He could put this label ‘excellence’ on it, was that he valued the birthright. Do we value it? Do you value your birthright? Do you value the fact, you dear young people, that you are born into an area where the light of God is known, where the work of God is seen, and where the saints are, our inheritance? This is no accident, “He hath chosen our inheritance

for us”; He has chosen it. So for all you dear young brothers and sisters, boys and girls, if God sees a boy or a girl who loves the company of the brethren, He loves that. If you have some interest in the truth I know how the brethren love it, and if we love it we can be sure that God loves it too.

If we see young persons beginning to make enquiries about God, that is evidence that God has begun His work. Then, too, if they love the brethren that is evidence that they have passed from death to life. So it is a good thing for young persons to look into themselves and see what is there, to see whether they have received the unction from the Holy One. They instinctively like to go to the meetings. I know some young brethren who consider it a penalty if they are not allowed to go to the meetings. Well, you may say, they just want to see the other young brethren. Well, suppose they do; there is nothing wrong with that. It shows there is some affinity; I do not mean a worldly one, or just a social one, but there is an affinity there in the work of God.

One of the next things we are told about Jacob is that he was obedient to his parents (Genesis 28: 7). He was a mature man then, so I am not just speaking only to the younger people now, I am speaking about the principle of obedience. Perhaps we have been a bit hard on Jacob, because God says about him that he was obedient to his parents in a most important matter, that is, marriage (see Genesis 22: 7). Now this is a vital matter for the young people that marriage must be in the Lord. Obedience must enter into it otherwise it is going to be disastrous. Esau saw that his parents were pleased with what Jacob had done and he did just the opposite. He chose a wife who was not in fellowship; that was not approved by his parents. Now, I know the young

people may be amused at this, but it is not a bad idea to ask your parents’ advice; you would like to be governed a good bit by their judgment in such an important matter as that, because it is an important matter.

So Jacob goes out, in obedience to his parents’ wish, to seek a wife in a limited circle. It is hard for young people, I know, to accept limitations, and it is hard for old people too. Each of us likes his own way, but it is specifically said in that section that Jacob obeyed his parents.

So he went out and what he found immediately was that he had God’s approval and was personally the object of the interest of heaven. What a wonderful thing to realise! His circumstances were difficult; he lay down and had a rock for a pillow—not a very comfortable one—but he got a wonderful appearing from God, as if God was approving him, approving the path of obedience in which he was, and God says, “I am with thee, and will keep thee”, Genesis 28: 15. What an assurance! And I can assure the young brethren that if you are moving on that path you can count on God’s support. He says, ‘I will be with you and I will bring to pass My thoughts for you’. ‘Oh’, you say, ‘I have not got much yet’, but God says, ‘I will bring it to pass; I will complete My work’, and He will. “He who has begun in you a good work will complete it unto Jesus Christ’s day”, Philippians 1: 6.

So then, as I say, Jacob is seeking a wife, and he comes across this flock of sheep. Then, what is even more interesting, he comes across this beautiful young woman. And the remarkable thing about it is that what affects him is that she belongs to the same family, the same kindred, she was “the daughter of Laban his mother’s brother”, Genesis 29: 10. It does not say he fell in love with her because of her beauty; it says he wept, he was greatly moved,

because of the sense of kindredship, the sense of family, and he kissed her and he wept. That is another thing about Jacob; he was a man who could weep, a man who had feelings. It says that God met with him and that he wept. “He wrestled with the Angel, and ... he wept” (see Hosea 12: 4). It does not tell us that in the history. It is a great thing to have this sense of family, this sense of kindredship, the sense that we are not part of a congregation but that we belong, and that we love, as we have already quoted, “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren”, 1 John 3: 14. So that is what marked Jacob, he had love for the family, you might say the divine family; it was the testimonial family, the family in which God was going to continue his testimony.

Then he considered for the sheep. That is another great thing; consider for the brethren, consider for what they need, consider for their refreshment. He took away the stone from the top of the well so that the water was made available. You know, the youngest brother in the meeting can do that; some of the best readings that we have are the result of a question from a young brother. A reading is not altogether a question of gift; of course gift enters into it, but it has been a concern with me whether we make enough room for what springs up out of the body of the brethren, particularly from the young brethren. Perhaps we are so busy getting on to our point and filling out what we have got before us that there is not room for the Spirit to get in, and yet there is a young brother there who has a question that is just the key question to, so to speak, take the covering off the well and get something fresh. So that we are not just coming together quoting the great worthies—we can do that to great advantage (but of course we could read them at home to great advantage)—but

we want to get more than that when we come together; we want to get something fresh and living and current. Where there is an honest enquiry we always get something. God will never overlook an honest enquiry.
When I was just a boy I used to find the meetings very difficult; I used to think, ‘Will I ever understand what they are talking about?’; it just seemed like Greek, and I told Mr. Lyon this.

Some of us here know what a man he was, and he said, ‘You know, Roy, every meeting, before you go, you ask the Lord for something and He will never fail you. There will always be a handful of purpose’. He was quoting from Ruth 2: 16. The Lord will always have something for you; you may not be able to give an outline of the reading, but you will get a handful, and if you get that, that is what you want, what you can hold in your hand.

There are some other features about Jacob here that are very important. He meets Esau, whom he had not treated rightly. He had slipped it over him (I suppose you use that expression here too) and he had to go through a great deal of exercise about it. He wrestled with God, he went to God about it. That is the thing to do if there is difficulty with a brother, go to God about it; and to quote dear Mr. Lyon again, he said, ‘You say, I have a difficulty?

Yes, you are the difficulty!’ That is what Jacob had to find out, that he was the trouble. God had something to say to him. As if God would say, ‘Never mind talking about Esau, I have something to say to you’, and He touched him on the spot where he needed to be touched. So instead of parading his wealth and showing how God had prospered him, he bowed himself seven times to the ground when he met Esau. What a way to gain a brother!

That is the solution to most difficulties, if there is someone willing to bow himself down seven times. That is a big order, is it not? You may say, ‘Well, I have been to see him once and I told him that I had not treated him just right, but he was pretty cool’. Well, Jacob bowed himself seven times, then he won the day. Esau did not say anything about the old trouble; he did not say, ‘You did me out of the blessing’. The fact is, of course, that Esau got some blessing too. God is so great; while Jacob got the blessing, Esau said, “Bless me—me also, my father!” (Genesis 27: 34), and God saw that he got a blessing too.

But what I wanted to draw attention to is what Esau said—Let us take our journey, and go on, and I will go before thee. And he (Jacob) said to him, My lord knows that the children are tender, and the suckling sheep and kine are with me; and if they should overdrive them only one day, all the flock would die. Let my lord, I pray thee, pass on before his servant, and I will drive on at my ease according to the pace of the cattle that is before me, and according to the pace of the children, until I come to my lord, to Seir”.

Now these are fine expressions; he says the children are tender. We have to remember that, dear brethren, about our children. We thank God for them, but we have to be careful with the children to avoid damaging them. It is not that you are unrighteous, no, but a child is a child, and it is often said, ‘You cannot put old heads on young shoulders’. So Jacob was a fatherly man. Abraham, of course, was a father outstandingly, from the standpoint of divine counsel and purpose, but Jacob was a family man practically. He had a large and a difficult family; he had a number of wives and he had a lot of difficulties with them too. Nevertheless, he was very considerate about the young, and we need to be. We do not want to

act in any way that will offend or hinder the young. The Lord indeed speaks very severely to anyone responsible for offending one of these little ones (see Matthew 18: 6). So we have to learn perhaps not to go quite so fast; we have to control ourselves somewhat in relation to the pace of the young. We may be clearer about things than they are; we must have a lot of patience.

If we read Jacob’s history we might not think he was a very patient man, and yet he was. He put up with a great deal from Laban, who was a difficult man. He changed Jacob’s wages ten times; I do not suppose it was a raise each time either, probably just the opposite, but he still went on serving him; and he had a lot of other difficulties. But what I am drawing attention to is the pace of the children. I am not saying that we should make wrong allowances for our young ones, but I do say that we must be patient. We must get down to their pace.

I speak very feelingly about this. I find it very hard to get near to young people, I might as well confess that. But some people do not, they get along fine with young people; I wish I had that ability. If we have not got it I think we should ask for it, to get to know the young ones, to get to understand their exercises. You might be surprised if you found out what some of them are going through. They may not say anything about it, but you get close to them and you will be surprised what exercises they are going through. So we have to get down to their pace. Then it mentions cattle, which reminds us that Jacob was a livestock man. He was not a mass production line man. A production line is no good in the assembly. Livestock teach you to have feelings. We have to deal with living persons, having living feelings and emotions and affections, and I am saying this humbly because I own that I fall short. I feel that, and I ask the Lord to help me,
and the Lord is helping me, I would say, to get nearer to the young ones, to get to know their names.

I have found that the young people value an interest; you remember their names, even remember what their hobbies are. You say, ‘Hobbies?’ Well, I know we must go easy on that, but still, what do they do in their spare time? What are they interested in? I feel sure if you have an interest in what they are interested in then you have a basis for trying to get them to be interested in what you are interested in. So we have to learn to go their pace. Jacob says, “I will drive on at my ease according to the pace of the cattle that is before me, and according to the pace of the children”. He also says, “If they should overdrive them only one day, all the flock would die”. It is a tragedy to overdrive. There is such a thing. We have been through a phase of that, overdriving; what tragedies have resulted from it!—divided homes, and the children saying they cannot put up with the pressure any longer. Thank God we have got help about that, and may we maintain the help that we have got.
In the end of Genesis Jacob really shines in his excellency. In Genesis 47 we read—“Joseph brought Jacob his father, and set him before Pharaoh”. What a scene that must have been!—

Joseph bringing up his old father, just a nomad! He would not have any insignia, or outward dignity, but he had divine dignity. Even then the excellency of Jacob was shining out. He was greater than Pharaoh: Scripture tells us that: “the inferior is blessed by the better”, Hebrews 7: 7. This great man, Joseph, is not ashamed of his father. Sometimes as men get on circumstantially they are ashamed of their fathers, but Joseph was not. He never forgot his father. He said to his brethren, “Is your father well—the old man of whom
ye spoke”, Genesis 43: 27. He always had his father in mind, just as the Lord was always thinking of His Father.

But now it is a question of dignity, bringing Jacob and setting him before Pharaoh, as if to say to Pharaoh, ‘There he is. What do you think of him? I know what I think of him’. Pharaoh might not have thought much of him. Still, he thought something of him because he was Joseph’s father, and so he said, ‘You can give him the best place in the land and do the best you can for him’. But Pharaoh could not patronise Jacob. You cannot patronise someone who is greater than you are, and that is the way the saints are. We do not need to be ashamed of being believers, we do not need to apologise, we do not need to feel that the world can patronise us, we are too great to be patronised. That is what the Lord said of His own—“They are not of the world, as I am not of the world”, John 17: 14. That is, you are too great to be worldly. The world cannot add anything to you because if you are a believer you are too great, and I think that was the case with Jacob here, that he was too great a man to be patronised by Pharaoh, and so the tables were reversed. Peter says, “Ye have been called to this (1 Peter 3: 9), called to inherit blessing, so that you are superior to the world in a spiritual sense. You have always got more than the greatest persons in the world have, so you are able to bless them.

So it says, “And Jacob blessed Pharaoh. And Pharaoh said to Jacob, How many are the days of the years of thy life? And Jacob said to Pharaoh, The days of the years of my sojourning are a hundred and thirty years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they do not attain to the days of the years of the life of my fathers, in the days of their sojourning”. Then again it says,

“And Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from Pharaoh”. He did not wait to be dismissed. If you were in the presence of a great dignitary and turned round and walked out, it would be an insult. You would have to wait to be dismissed; but Jacob did not wait to be dismissed. He was in charge of the situation. Poor old man as he was outwardly, yet what was dignified was there; it was the excellency of Jacob shining out, refinement, the work of God. There had been all the ups and downs, the heat by day and the cold by night, all the different things that he had had to meet, all the days that he says were few and evil, but what a result from it all!
So may it be with us, dear brethren; our days are only few and evil at the best, but in spite of all that Jacob went through the work of God in its excellency was there and it could go on.

And it does go on and we can be conscious of being dignified persons, because the greatest dignity of all is to be sons of God. That is what we are, sons of God, and so we can bless, and we can be before God, as Jacob is at the end of the chapter, as worshippers. That involves sonship and kinship and the liberty of the family, and dignity. So it says, “And Israel worshipped on the bed’s head”. He did not die in weakness, he filled out his days. He says they were few and evil, but they were full to the very last one, and he went out in glory—
“Israel worshipped”. It is Israel now; that is, the Jacob side comes to equality with the purpose side. There is not any disparity; he is equal to the new name that God had given him.

Well, that is the greatest privilege we have, beloved brethren, the greatest dignity that we have. And it is not separated from the practical testings of the ways of God with us. It is the product of that. So it comes to light; you can tell in a

brother’s part in the service of God what substance he has in his soul, what he has gained in his exercises in the ways of God, the glorious result of the sufferings and the testings, all brought out in the dignity of a son. It is really what you have in Jacob at the end—Israel—his new name. So in the service of God we can abstract ourselves from all the difficulties and all the sorrows and all the pressures and we can be in God’s presence in complete liberty and dignity, in freedom to worship. God is seeking it—“The Father seeks such as his worshippers”, John 4: 23. What a favour it is, what a reward it is, to touch that in any measure and thus arrive substantially at God’s end in His ways with us. May He bless the word.

It is a matter to be observed and considered that men of God should have such thoughts in regard to the greatness and majesty of God, speaking of Him as “the Same”, the self-existent One (see note to Deuteronomy 32: 39), and as Moses himself speaks here “from eternity to eternity thou art God” (verse 2). Linked with such thoughts there is a sense of the brevity of human life. You see it with Moses here and with Hezekiah in Isaiah 37, which we considered in the earlier meeting. It would appear that the Spirit would stress the importance of applying our brief sojourn here to a deeper understanding of the greatness of God. Jacob said, “Few and evil have been the

days of the years of my life”, Genesis 4: 7: 9. Perhaps he was thinking of the years in Padan-Aram, the death of Rachel, the disgrace of Judah, and the loss of Joseph, but later he could speak of “The God that shepherded me all my life long to this day”, Genesis 48: 15. So the Spirit would impress on us the need to devote our days to acquiring a knowledge of God.

There are certain daily matters spoken of in Scripture. The manna was gathered daily (Exodus 16: 4), with the instruction for the double supply on the sixth day (v.5). How important it is to gather the manna daily as imparting to us the grace of Christ. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily (Acts 17: 11). They not only read the Scriptures—they searched them. How good to search the Scriptures and find some of the treasures of the greatness of God as revealed in Christ.

Then Paul separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the school of Tyrannus (Acts 19: 9). It emphasizes the importance of daily coming under Paul’s teaching as to the greatness of the mystery as unfolded in the Ephesian epistle. An exercised believer would thus regulate his days rightly, balancing legitimate things like work and leisure so that he increases in his knowledge of the greatness of God.

The deep feelings of our Lord expressed in Psalm 102: 23–28 affect our spirits—“My God, take me not away in the midst of my days!” (verse 24). One has been impressed that in John’s gospel the conclusion of the Lord’s pathway is marked in days. The resurrection of Lazarus came at the end of the Lord’s pathway. It would appear that the cry of verse 24 of Psalm 102
would imply all that lay upon Him as having to go into death to break its power. How beautifully that psalm concludes in extolling
the greatness of God—“the Same”.

In Psalm 90 Moses is the minister concerned as to the needs of the testimony. He was given the pattern of the tabernacle; the responsibility was laid upon him to see that it was adhered to (Exodus 25: 9, etc.). Each day would be numbered as he exercised oversight as to the building of God’s dwelling. Then what burden he carried, what discipline he experienced.
The care of divine interests brings its own peculiar discipline. He knew, however, the God who was “from eternity to eternity” and asks Him to “establish ... the work of our hands”

(Psalm 90: 17). Paul spoke of the burden of all the assemblies pressing upon him daily, but could speak of the greatness of God as One able to do “far exceedingly above all which we ask or think”, Ephesians 3: 20.
We should, therefore, number our days. Life is brief (v.10). The poet said, When as a child I laughed and wept,
Time crept;
When as a youth I dreamed and talked,
Time walked;
When I became a full-grown man,
Time ran;
When older still I daily grew,
Time flew;
Soon I shall find as travelling on,
Time gone, eternity begun.
May we make the best use of our days!

I have been impressed, as we have been listening to what has been said, as to what Naomi had. As we know from the history, her husband had died, and then her sons died. She was in a land of famine, a land where outwardly everything was against her, where there was no resource, where what she had leaned on for support had been entirely removed, no masculine comfort whatever. But it appears from what Ruth said, and from what the Spirit of God records, that she had at least three things: she had a God, she had her people, and she had a relation, a mighty man of wealth. And as we have been taught, Naomi really is expressive of the assembly in days of brokenness, in days when things are publicly weak and of no account with men, indeed passed by without any recognition. Naomi is a figure of weakness, a figure outwardly to be pitied because of what is lacking; and that is what the assembly publicly has come to—the church publicly in breakdown. You think of what it was in the pristine day, the unity that was there, the resource that was there, what the service of God must have—been, and the speaking of the Spirit when all were together and had all things common—what a time it was! But it lasted only a very brief while before discord and disintegration began to come in, and we have seen this extended right down to our day.
But then Naomi and all that she speaks of is not without resource—she is not without what properly belongs to her; and Ruth the Moabitess the gentile, who had no claim, and yet who was

stimulated by affection and an appreciation of the worth that was there in Naomi—recognises what Naomi has, and she says, “Whither thou goest I will go, and where thou lodgest I will lodge—thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God”. Whatever else Naomi lacked she had her people, and she had her God. She had her own people, as our brother has been saying (see March 1979 issue p.14), she had those to whom she could go, with whom she had an affinity, who loved and appreciated her. Whatever her failings, whatever the breakdown, whatever the departure, there were those that belonged to her, those that she had a right to go to, and those who would appreciate and recognise the claim that she had over them. No doubt Ruth had not met them; she had only heard by report; but to say that “thy people shall be my people” means that she senses that there is something of great value there, something that is for her comfort, for her encouragement and for her building up in resource and strength and wealth, that these people that Naomi had were available for her to lay claim to. In a sense she had not been invited; you might say, What temerity to lay claim to this. But then Ruth had a right—as all those that are found washing their robes have a right—a “right to the tree of life”
(Revelation 22: 14); and Ruth had a right to all the resource and power and comfort that were to be found in Naomi’s people.

And then, “thy God my God”—what a resource that was, that Naomi had a God. Ruth evidently had been acquainted with her for some years—she must have been—and yet perhaps until this moment of testing came, the true value and worth of Naomi’s God had not dawned in her soul. However, when she sees Naomi retracing her steps, going back out of Moab towards Bethlehem, anticipating the wealth of a city where there was food, the light of what Naomi’s God could be to her dawned on her.

And this is what the assembly has. The assembly has, even in days of brokenness and weakness, a unique appreciation of God Himself that no other family has, the appreciation of the resource that there is in God. So she found as she clung to Naomi, as she joined with her, followed her lead, went in her steps, took this way over the Jordan and came to Bethlehem, the place where the Lord Himself was born, “little to be among the thousands of Judah”

(Micah 5: 2), that the appreciation of what God was to Naomi deepened in her. Thus Ruth is found in full association with Naomi, clinging to her, going in her steps in a way of faith, not fully knowing where she was going because this was a new way to Ruth, she had not been this way before; but she was going away content to leave Moab and to enter into the small confines of Bethlehem in the reproach of association with one who had lost everything publicly. She was drawn into it by the recognition of the fact that Naomi’s God was the source, the power, and the fulness of all that she found comfort in.

But then she goes a stage further, because she discovers that Naomi not only had this, but that she also had a relation who was a mighty man of wealth. What treasure he had under his hand!—what food supply; the immenseness of the barley and the wheat that were his; the fields were his, the product was his, the reapings were his. The gleanings he left for others, but the sum of the wealth was his—a mighty man of wealth.

Well, Ruth hears of this and goes on until she is brought into full association with this mighty man of wealth; but she arrives at it by association with Naomi. Typically she finds through the assembly what Christ really is as a provider of food. One who can elevate her above all that she had ever dreamt of or lived for. She finds that this

mighty man of wealth is going to raise her up and set on a line of things that brings in the worshipper and brings in David and Solomon. Think of Ruth thus becoming productive of that great royal line that goes on to Christ.

These passages came to mind, as complementing perhaps what our brothers have said, as to what Naomi had, whatever she might appear to be outwardly. As in touch with her and in vital contact with the life that is there she brings into expression and shares these things that she has—her people, her God, and the mighty man of wealth. Well, let us appreciate the assembly in this way as bringing us into the enjoyment of this vast area of resource, for His name’s sake.

We had a touch on Lord’s day, beloved brethren, as to Genesis 1: 2, “And the earth was waste and empty, and darkness was on the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters”. What a matter that is as we think of the anticipative view that the Spirit had in regard to the whole area of things where the divine will was to be worked out, ‘ hovering’, anticipating what would emerge, suppose the fulfilment of matters was when the Spirit as a dove descended on Christ. At that point the whole divine will in its conception was seen in its totality, a Man in relation to God
upon whom the Spirit of God could descend and abide upon Him.

I read these scriptures as thinking about this matter. The Spirit, in type, in Genesis 24 is, you might say, on the outlook in regard to what is emerging for the divine will. It is not in any forceful, arbitrary way; the features here are patience and dependence and along with that a complete committal to what was pleasing to God. It is interesting that these are exactly the features that come to light in Rebecca. I think the Spirit was looking for this consonance, an affinity with the Spirit in affirmation of the way that He was on as to what was coming to light. It would speak to us, I believe, beloved brethren, as to what the Spirit of God is bringing out as to features of the assembly and how there is response, by His touch, to Christ.

So there would be joy in our hearts as we think how the Spirit is looking for this—we might say, is helping us that it might be so—and as soon as these features emerged in Rebecca, there was that moment when, as it says in verse 21, “the man was astonished at her, remaining silent …”. It is just as though the whole thing had emerged under the Spirit in the patience that He had exhibited and in the dependence that He had shown, and yet it had all come to light under the touch that He knew would be pleasing to the Master.

Beloved brethren, what a moment we are in, the Spirit’s day; not a day when everything is going just the way we might want it to go, but rather a matter of our dependence on the ability of the Spirit to bring to light that which is pleasing to Christ and to God. What a matter this is for us in the alertness that should increasingly mark us in regard to the opportunities of this the Spirit’s day. This young woman was energetic. She “ran”, it says. I suppose the danger always is with us

that we settle down to a complacent way of thinking about things. I think the Spirit rejoiced in the energy that this young woman exhibited and her willingness in answering the question that was put to her, “Wilt thou go with this man?” How she responded! Beloved brethren, let us have the consciousness in our hearts that there is that under His touch which, as we would seek to be dependent upon Him, would bring confirmation in our own souls that the pathway we are on is right. When we come to that, other things will maybe not trouble us quite so much. May the young people with us get some touch in their souls, in the power of the Spirit, as to the glory of the present moment.
When we turn to Mark’s gospel, the Lord had taken up very many matters in the chapters prior to where we have read. In Mark 11: 11 He “looked round on all things” and later
“entering into the temple, he began to cast out those who sold and who bought in the temple”

(Mark 11: 15). How jealous He was, and is, as to what is due to God. The Lord has had to say, and has the right to say, to things in this setting. In our experience we have had to learn and re-learn this. He “sat down opposite the treasury”; I think it would be a touch for us, on the lines of my exercise, that the Lord was just waiting to see what would emerge. The disciples were close alongside because it says. He “called his disciples”, but they are not the focal point at this moment. There was something for them to be instructed in just before He went out from the temple in chapter 13. What a moment this is then as the Lord waits anticipatively to see what would emerge and, despite all the antagonism and the contradiction of the Pharisees and the Sadducees and all that kind of thing, there emerges in this woman a person who is marked by features of the Lord Jesus in preparedness to give everything she had. O, beloved brethren, how our hearts should warm as to

what is seen in perfection in Christ, ‘reserving nothing’, as we sometimes sing, ‘save the right to love’ (hymn 318). In character the same feature is in this woman. It is what was in the Lord Jesus personally, in the path of suffering and sorrow that He was on and, in some measure at least, there was an answer to it in this woman’s heart. “She of her destitution”, the Lord says, “has cast in all that she had, the whole of her living”. It has been well said, often said, she could have kept one of these coins, but she cast them both in. What a moment this is then and we should be encouraged as we have come together in this way that the Lord would speak to our hearts afresh that He is anticipatively watching and looking to see what is emerging in the power of the Spirit in response to Himself—and how He appreciates it!

Now just a touch as to Deuteronomy 32. This is a fine chapter in the maturity of Moses, a man in relation to God. The faithfulness of God is borne witness to here by Moses himself, how He had brought the people through and what was in the people for God, “For Jehovah’s portion is his people”, and how the faithfulness of God had seen them through in the “waste, howling wilderness; he compassed him about, he watched over him, he preserved him as the apple of his eye”. Then it goes on to say, “As the eagle stirreth up its nest, hovereth over its young, spreadeth out its wings, taketh them, beareth them on its feathers”. God has been faithful in regard to what is here in relation to the divine Name. What Moses is saying is that God has been a Father to us in this setting. A brother mentioned in the prayer meeting last night that Philip could ask the Lord, “Show us the Father”, and Jesus answered, “He that has seen me has seen the Father”, John 14: 8, 9. What has been seen in Christ is just the same in the Father, that

ability to carry through everything in this attractive way. So the exercise would be raised in our hearts, what sort of features are there amongst us? Can we look after things on the line of these verses we have read together?

“The eagle stirreth up its nest”—we had a word a week ago about the discipline that comes in, and that would have a result like this, that there would be a stirring up. If we take things from the Father in that regard there will be “the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those exercised by it”, Hebrews 12: 11. But along with that, beloved brethren, may I say again, we so easily settle down into a routine of things. What it is to get stirred up in our affections so that there are desires and exercises raised with us all on the lines of ‘hovering over its young’.

The whole potential in life is there, especially so in our young people, and family affections and care would be aroused to see that that potential might come to full fruition. This calls for watchfulness which is essentially a fatherly feature. You might say that was Paul in relation to the Corinthians. He was just watching how they were going to act. He did not want to come in amongst them because he knew he might have, as it were, to lay the law down, but he was watching to see how they would conduct themselves. “Ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet not many fathers” (1 Corinthians 4: 15)—he was one of the fathers; he says that, and they had to acknowledge it, and what a fatherly spirit was exhibited by him. So the word in relation to the fathers is, “Ye have known him that is from the beginning”, 1 John 2: 13.
What experience have we of the Father’s touch with us and can we relate it to the generations that are coming on?
Then there is an ability to lead into where there is fruitfulness and where there is that which

will sustain us and keep us. Maybe the outward look of things is not always so attractive, but what is within? You might never think of getting “honey out of the crag” or “oil out of the flinty rock”, but that is what is there, and that is what the fathers would bring out, so that there is sustenance and a food supply leading us on in relation to the whole privilege side of things where, as we read in Deuteronomy 32: 14, everything is in abundance.

These are the few thoughts I had, beloved brethren. May we be encouraged as to this so that we might get a quickening touch as we come together. I believe that is the whole contrast in a gathering like this compared with anything else that is happening in the city at this very moment. The Spirit of God, the Lord Jesus, and the Father would bring in a quickening touch, so that we realise that we are connected with that which is going through, related to the divine will and arrangement; and may our committals be all the more real on this line of dependence, patience, devotion, and watchfulness, for His name’s sake.

Love never fails. I am certain that love, if it existed, would never allow an issue to be carried over years or months. It never fails. This verse (Matthew 18: 19) contemplates two conditions that heaven recognises. First, two saints agreed, and second, praying to God. Heaven recognises them—the Father does and answers it for them—not for the assembly—for them.
